analysis.one_liner: Bans brand-name drug companies from paying generic makers to delay cheaper competition.
analysis.headline: A bipartisan bill to stop 'pay-for-delay' drug settlements cleared the Senate Judiciary Committee favorably on April 10, 2025, and now sits on the Senate calendar awaiting a floor vote that has not been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: When a generic drug company challenges a brand-name drug's patents, the brand company sometimes settles by paying the generic maker to stay off the market for years — a 'reverse payment' that keeps prices high. This bill makes such deals presumptively illegal, lets the Federal Trade Commission sue and impose penalties up to three times the value transferred, and requires drug companies to certify to the FTC and Justice Department that they disclosed their complete settlement terms, including side deals and oral promises. It still allows legitimate settlements, such as an agreed early entry date or payment of reasonable litigation costs.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients and taxpayers. Cheaper generic drugs and biosimilars would reach the market sooner instead of being held back by settlements in which a brand company pays a would-be competitor to delay. The bill's own findings note generics average 80-85% discounts off brand prices and that federal dollars cover over 40% of the roughly $450 billion spent on retail prescription drugs each year, so taxpayers share directly in the savings.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and taxpayers who buy prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: It prohibits patent settlements between brand and generic or biosimilar manufacturers that have anticompetitive effects, and presumes a settlement is anticompetitive whenever the generic or biosimilar filer receives anything of value and agrees to stay out of the market for any period.

It gives the FTC a direct enforcement tool, including civil actions and civil penalties capped at three times the value transferred, and strips a generic maker's 180-day marketing exclusivity if it participates in a violating deal.

It closes disclosure gaps: CEOs or the negotiating official must certify to the FTC and the Justice Department that filings include the complete agreement, related side agreements, and written descriptions of any oral promises, so regulators can see what was actually traded.

It leaves normal settlements alone: paying for an earlier entry date, covering reasonable litigation expenses (up to $7.5 million in 2025, adjusted for inflation), a covenant not to sue, or any deal whose procompetitive benefits outweigh the anticompetitive harm remain permitted.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers lose their ability to preserve monopoly profits by paying potential generic and biosimilar competitors to delay market entry. Generic and biosimilar makers lose the side payments those deals offered, though most would gain earlier access to markets they were being paid to avoid.

drawbacks.text: The presumption of illegality attaches to any deal where a generic filer gets 'anything of value' and agrees to any delay, even a short one, which could chill settlements that are actually procompetitive — the bill tries to manage this with a preponderance-of-the-evidence defense and specific exclusions, but some lawful, efficiency-producing settlements may be deterred.

Payments for litigation expenses are capped at $7.5 million in 2025 with inflation adjustments, which may be too low for complex pharmaceutical patent cases and could push parties away from settling altogether, meaning more prolonged litigation instead of earlier generic entry.

The bill applies only to agreements entered into after enactment, so existing pay-for-delay settlements are untouched, and enforcement depends on FTC action within a six-year window from the certification filing.

Critics of prior versions of this approach have argued that not every value transfer harms consumers — for example, paying a generic maker to launch early as an authorized generic can increase competition — which is why the bill directs the FTC to report within a year on whether to add an additional exclusion for damage-claim releases.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are large and well-documented in the bill's own findings: generic drugs cost 80-85% less than brand versions, and settlements that pay competitors to delay entry keep high prices in place for years, at direct cost to patients, insurers, and taxpayers. The main costs are legal — some legitimate settlements may become harder to strike, and complex cases may end up litigated longer. On balance, a targeted ban with built-in exclusions and a procompetitive defense is a reasonable design, and the safeguards address the strongest objection rather than ignoring it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on March 24, 2025, referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, reported favorably on April 10, 2025 with an amendment, and placed on the Senate's legislative calendar — but no floor vote has been scheduled.

narrative.text: Senator Klobuchar introduced S. 1096 with a bipartisan group including Senators Grassley, Durbin, Cramer, Blumenthal, Ernst, Welch, Kelly, and Booker on March 24, 2025.
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.

On April 3, 2025, the committee ordered the bill reported favorably with an amendment in the nature of a substitute, and on April 10 it was formally reported by Senator Grassley and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders as Calendar No. 46.
The bill drew eight cosponsors — five of 45 Senate Democrats and three of 55 Senate Republicans — and cleared committee on a bipartisan basis, but it has not received a floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, brand-name drug companies, since the current rules that let them pay competitors to delay cheaper drugs remain in place while the bill waits on the Senate calendar.

for.name: Sen. Amy Klobuchar
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and assembled a bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
for.what_they_did: Signed on as an original cosponsor and formally reported the bill out of committee with an amendment in the nature of a substitute on April 10, 2025.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was introduced by a Democrat and reported out of committee by the committee's Republican chair, with cosponsors split five Democrats and three Republicans; no senator has acted against it in the record.

industries.note: These companies use reverse-payment settlements to share monopoly profits with would-be competitors and keep cheaper versions off the market; the bill would make that strategy illegal and expose violators to penalties of up to three times the value transferred.

They would forfeit the lucrative side payments brands currently offer for delaying entry, but would gain earlier access to markets where generics sell at 80-85% discounts — and they keep the right to sue under antitrust laws.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee with bipartisan support and sits on the Senate calendar, which in practice means it waits for the majority leader to schedule floor time. Prior versions of this same pay-for-delay legislation cleared committee in earlier Congresses and never received a Senate floor vote, and drug-industry opposition has historically been intense, so the most likely path is that it stalls on the calendar unless leadership prioritizes it.
